messages.subject_clean: [brms-users] Question about multilevel ordinal model using brms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

I have a question about proportional odds (PO) assumption. How can I do parallel test in brms? And if I find some categorical predictors violate the PO assumption, how can I modify the function in brms?

For example, Y is an ordinal response variable with range [1:5], X is a categorical predictor with range [1:3], with common coefficient, Y~X+(1 | District). If the parallel test shows X violates the PO assumption and need to assign separate coefficients, how can I modify the function in brms? And can I test its random effect in brms (e.g. Y~X+(X | District) ) ?

P.S.: I have tried R2MLwiN package to do the parallel test. And with common coefficient, the function is logit(Y, cons, 5) ~ 1 + X[1:4] + (1[1:4] | District); with separate coefficients, the function is logit(Y, cons, 5) ~ 1 + X + (1[1:4] | District).

Thanks and regards.

Diva

Hi Paul,

I have another question. It is about the coefficients of group-level effects. I have applied brms as well as clmm packages to model a 2-level ordinal regression.

For brms, the result shows as :
Group-Level Effects:
~DISTRICT:SUBDISTRICT (Number of levels: 115)

                  Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat

sd(Intercept)     2.22      0.19         1.88     2.63         2432       1.00

For clmm, the result shows as :
Random effects:
 Groups Name                Variance Std.Dev.
SUBDISTRICT(Intercept)    4.595    2.144
Number of groups:  SUBDISTRICT 115

Therefore, just wander if sd(Intercept) in brms corresponds to Std.Dev of intercept in clmm. And if so, how can I extract the variance of intercept in brms?

Thanks and regards.

Diva

messages.body_plain:
Regarding the PO question: I don't think you can do this test in brms and you can't fit separate coefficients (I call them category specific effects) with the cumulative() family, since it may lead to negative probabilities.

If you want to fit category specific effects, use family sratio(), cratio(), or acat() and write cs(X).

Regarding your 2. question: To get the means of all the random effects variances, you can use, for instance, colMeans(posterior_samples(<your model object>, pars = "^sd_"))

messages.subject: Bayesian Network model with mixed variable types using brms
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian Network model with mixed variable types using brms
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

First of all, thank you so much Paul-Christian for developing brms. As a newbie to Bayesian statistics, stan and MLM, the package is very helpful in facilitating the learning process. Originally starting with JAGS, I'd like to move over to brms/stan for my Bayesian Network model with mixed variable types (continuous/discrete).
>From reading the different vignettes of brms and the stan manual, I think it should be possible to parametrize such a network in brms but I'm having a hard-time conceptualizing it. Maybe someone here has tried something similar and can point me into the right direction.

In a Bayesian Network the network structure and the directed graphs define the (in)dependencies between random variables. In my example the different nodes are connected through regression models. Figure 1 shows the structure of my network (see attachment). My dependent variable rloss represents a relative loss proportion ranging from 0 (no loss) to 1 (completely destroyed). The data is sort of beta-distributed with a high probability density close to 0 (see Figure 2). In addition there are about 10% of cases in my dataset which are exactly zero. From reading Andrew Gelman's suggestion in this post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/6wIuJJk1km4/Y-Z4X_o_CQAJ> in the stan user group, I could first model a latent variable 'dam' that represents the probability of rloss being either 0 or some value different from 0 using logistic regression. Another option is using a mixture model. For that I'm re-designing rloss, where I add 1€ to each absolute loss value before normalizing it with the total value for each case to get the proportion for rloss. By doing that, I'm getting rid of cases that are exactly zero and I can log-transform rloss. After the log transformation, I get two normal distributions, where one distribution represents the cases that originally ran from >0 to 1 and the ones that are 0 (see Figure 3). I've implemented the latter in a brms model, which seems to work fine for two predictors (wst and con) for the distributions and one predictor for proportion of the mixture. However, the model doesn't converge when I add the variable 'd' for predicting the distribution and the mixture.

Questions:

1) Given the structure of my response variable, which of the two options (logistic regression or mixture model) would make more sense to implement using brms?

2) Is there a good way to put the "hierachical" or stacked structure of the network model in brms by combining multiple regression models? E.g. in the current example: model wst through a regression with rfi and then use wst to model rloss etc.

3) When making predictions for rloss, I might not have data or evidence for all predictors (nodes in the network). Is there a way in brms to make predictions with incomplete observations by using the underlying distribution function for the missing data point?

#data
> head(data)

> summary(data)

#mixture model

mix_rloss <- mixture(gaussian, gaussian)
prior_rloss <- c(
  prior(normal(-14, 10), Intercept, dpar = mu1),
  prior(normal(-5, 10), Intercept, dpar = mu2))

fit_rloss <- brm(bf(log_rloss ~ wst + con,  theta2 ~ wst),
            data=data, family = mix_rloss, prior = prior_rloss,
            inits = 0, chains = 2, iter=3000)

#does not converge:
fit_rloss1 <- brm(bf(log_rloss ~ wst + con + log_d,  theta2 ~ wst + log_d),
            data=data, family = mix_rloss, prior = prior_rloss,
            inits = 0, chains = 2, iter=3000)

pp_check(fit_rloss) #see Figure_4 in the attachment

messages.subject: speeding up model comparisons
messages.subject_clean: speeding up model comparisons
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,
 I've run a couple test models that I'd like to compare:

result ~ 1    vs
result ~ ( 1 | ID )

to see if the random term improves the model.

Result is binomial, n=36,000, and ID= 19,000 levels

The models like this (without all the smooth terms I've mentioned in my last post) run quickly enough using multi-core, but R crashes if I don't use pointwise comparison for WAIC or LOOIC. This is true even on the best computer I have available, which is an an 8 core / 3.5 GHz computer with 32 GB of RAM.

The pointwise WAIC comparison has taken around 12 hours and still isn't complete. Is this to be expected? Is there a way the pointwise comparison could be done with parallel processing to speed it up?

Thanks,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
It could be made in parallel, but this likely had to be implemented in the loo package rather than in brms.

You could reduce the number of posterior samples involved in the comparisons, to make stuff fit into RAM by using the nsamples or subset argument of LOO.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Viktor,

1) have you thought of using the zero_inflated_beta family for your data?

2) brms is not yet able to fit multivariate models except for multivariate normal ones, but this will be implemented in the future.

3) This is not yet possible in brms.

Given the kind of model you want to fit, I am not sure if brms should be your package of choice. Maybe you can start with the Stan code brms provides and build your own Stan model based on that.

Originally starting with JAGS, I'd like to move over to brms/stan for my Bayesian Network model with mixed variable types (continuous/discrete).
> From reading the different vignettes of brms and the stan manual, I think it should be possible to parametrize such a network in brms but I'm having a hard-time conceptualizing it. Maybe someone here has tried something similar and can point me into the right direction.

> In a Bayesian Network the network structure and the directed graphs define the (in)dependencies between random variables. In my example the different nodes are connected through regression models. Figure 1 shows the structure of my network (see attachment). My dependent variable rloss represents a relative loss proportion ranging from 0 (no loss) to 1 (completely destroyed). The data is sort of beta-distributed with a high probability density close to 0 (see Figure 2). In addition there are about 10% of cases in my dataset which are exactly zero. From reading Andrew Gelman's suggestion in this post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/6wIuJJk1km4/Y-Z4X_o_CQAJ> in the stan user group, I could first model a latent variable 'dam' that represents the probability of rloss being either 0 or some value different from 0 using logistic regression. Another option is using a mixture model. For that I'm re-designing rloss, where I add 1€ to each absolute loss value before normalizing it with the total value for each case to get the proportion for rloss. By doing that, I'm getting rid of cases that are exactly zero and I can log-transform rloss. > > > From reading the different vignettes of brms and the stan manual, I think it should be possible to parametrize such a network in brms but I'm having a hard-time conceptualizing it. Maybe someone here has tried something similar and can point me into the right direction.
> > >
> > > In a Bayesian Network the network structure and the directed graphs define the (in)dependencies between random variables. In my example the different nodes are connected through regression models. Figure 1 shows the structure of my network (see attachment). My dependent variable rloss represents a relative loss proportion ranging from 0 (no loss) to 1 (completely destroyed). The data is sort of beta-distributed with a high probability density close to 0 (see Figure 2). In addition there are about 10% of cases in my dataset which are exactly zero. From reading Andrew Gelman's suggestion in this post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/6wIuJJk1km4/Y-Z4X_o_CQAJ> in the stan user group, I could first model a latent variable 'dam' that represents the probability of rloss being either 0 or some value different from 0 using logistic regression. Another option is using a mixture model. For that I'm re-designing rloss, where I add 1€ to each absolute loss value before normalizing it with the total value for each case to get the proportion for rloss. By doing that, I'm getting rid of cases that are exactly zero and I can log-transform rloss. After the log transformation, I get two normal distributions, where one distribution represents the cases that originally ran from >0 to 1 and the ones that are 0 (see Figure 3). I've implemented the latter in a brms model, which seems to work fine for two predictors (wst and con) for the distributions and one predictor for proportion of the mixture. However, the model doesn't converge when I add the variable 'd' for predicting the distribution and the mixture.

> > >
> > > 2) Is there a good way to put the "hierachical" or stacked structure of the network model in brms by combining multiple regression models? E.g. in the current example: model wst through a regression with rfi and then use wst to model rloss etc.
> > >
> > > 3) When making predictions for rloss, I might not have data or evidence for all predictors (nodes in the network). Is there a way in brms to make predictions with incomplete observations by using the underlying distribution function for the missing data point?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

Thank you for your reply. I have reviewed some instructions of other packages in R. And I think a possible solution to explore the category specific coefficients is to build up several dummy variables (one for each category). That is to say, since X has four categories, then I could create x1, x2, x3, x4 as dummy variables and explore the coefficient of each of them through cumulative link logit model. Do you think it is a possible way? Many thanks.

Diva

在 2017年10月2日星期一 UTC+8下午6:52:04，Paul Buerkner写道：

> Regarding the PO question: I don't think you can do this test in brms and you can't fit separate coefficients (I call them category specific effects) with the cumulative() family, since it may lead to negative probabilities.
>
> If you want to fit category specific effects, use family sratio(), cratio(), or acat() and write cs(X).
>
> Regarding your 2. question: To get the means of all the random effects variances, you can use, for instance, colMeans(posterior_samples(<your model object>, pars = "^sd_"))
>

Hi Paul,

I think the solution I proposed can only be used when adding a categorical specific random slope.

And I have used LOO to compare a random intercept model (RI) and a random slope random intercept model (RSRI) based on the same dataset, the result as below shows that SE is very large. I don't know if this comparison is valid or something wrong with my model. P.S.: Each RSRI model only considers random effects of one variable from Var1-5.

（RI — RSRI） LOOIC SE
Var1 -1.07772 8.220301
Var2 0.540573 6.018782
Var3 -4.536884 1.80831
Var4 0.689996 4.367917
Var5 41.3646 18.74543

Regards.

Diva

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

The code for RI model is :

brmf0<-bf("Response ~ Var1 + Var2 + Var3 + Var4 + Var5 + (1 | DISTRICT:SUBDISTRICT)")
fit0<-brm(brmf0, data = mydata, family=cumulative("logit"), threshold="flexible", control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9), iter=5000, warmup=1000, thin=3)

The code for RSRI model is: (take Var1, Var2 as examples, actually doing a loop to explore the random effects of each Var)
brmf1<-bf("Response ~ Var1 + Var2 + Var3 + Var4 + Var5 + (Var1 | DISTRICT:SUBDISTRICT)")
fit1<-brm(brmf1, data = mydata, family=cumulative("logit"), threshold="flexible", control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9), iter=5000, warmup=1000, thin=3)
LOO(fit0, fit1)

fit0-fit1            LOOIC           SE
Var1             -1.07772       8.220301

brmf2<-bf("Response ~ Var1 + Var2 + Var3 + Var4 + Var5 + (Var2 | DISTRICT:SUBDISTRICT)")
fit2<-brm(brmf2, data = mydata, family=cumulative("logit"), threshold="flexible", control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9), iter=5000, warmup=1000, thin=3)
LOO(fit0, fit2)

fit0-fit2            LOOIC            SE
Var2              0.540573      6.018782

....
....
....

P.S.: Var1-Var5 are all categorical variables, Var1(four categories), Var2(two categories), Var3(two categories), Var4(two categories), Var5(six categories)

Thanks and regards.

Diva

Hi Paul,

Thanks for your reply. The model I used in brms is cumulative link logit model. And as you mentioned before, I think it's impossible to model category specific effects because it may cause negative probability. And now my question is why the SE is so large when I use LOO( ) to compare the slope random random intercept (RSRI) model and the only random intercept (RI) model. Thanks. The two models I compared are as below:

The code for RI model is :

brmf0<-bf("Response ~ Var1 + Var2 + Var3 + Var4 + Var5 + (1 | DISTRICT:SUBDISTRICT)")
fit0<-brm(brmf0, data = mydata, family=cumulative("logit"), threshold="flexible", control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9), iter=5000, warmup=1000, thin=3)

brmf1<-bf("Response ~ Var1 + Var2 + Var3 + Var4 + Var5 + (Var1 | DISTRICT:SUBDISTRICT)")
fit1<-brm(brmf1, data = mydata, family=cumulative("logit"), threshold="flexible", control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9), iter=5000, warmup=1000, thin=3)

LOO(fit0, fit2)

fit0-fit2            LOOIC            SE
Var2              0.540573      6.018782

....
....
....

P.S.: Var1-Var5 are all categorical variables, Var1(four categories), Var2(two categories), Var3(two categories), Var4(two categories), Var5(six categories)

Regards.

Diva

messages.subject: Calculating group means from model coefficients - Is there a quick way to do it?
messages.subject_clean: Calculating group means from model coefficients - Is there a quick way to do it?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've finally been persuaded to switch from Python to R for fitting regression models because BRMS is so awesomel!!

However, i'm a little rusty with R, so this is a noob question.

What I would like to be able to do is quickly calculate means of every level of multiple factors quickly, in order to do hypothesis testing and plotting.

Let me clarify with an example. Say a have data set with two factors, each with two levels:

data = data.frame(
    A = rep(c("A1", "A2"), each = 10),
    B = c("B1", "B2"),
    Y = rnorm(20, 0, 1)
)

I then fit a simple fixed effects model using brms,

post1 = brm(Y ~ A * B, data = data)

Now I can extract the posterior samples for the fixed effects,

feff = head(posterior_samples(post1, 'b'))

and it would look something like this:

  b_Intercept      b_AA2     b_BB2  b_AA2:BB2
1  -1.3444522 0.99164610 1.2801640 -1.3762587
2  -0.8593994 0.55953183 0.9143220 -0.7234478
3  -0.6114819 0.25175212 0.2485278 -0.3393085
4  -0.6324323 0.08866249 0.5348998 -0.4742578

Now say if I wanted to calculate the group mean for A1:B2, i would sum across the "b_Intercept" and "b_BB2" columns. Or I could multiply each row by c(1, 0, 1, 0).

Another way I could do this it to call,

 hypothesis(post1, "Intercept + BB2 = 0")

which returns the mean estimate and intervals.

What I'd like to know is if there is a quick way of obtaining the samples. For example, is there a function that would let me say something like:

get_identity_vector(A = A1, B = B2) which would return c(1,0,1,0). Manually specifying the vector is quite time consuming once there are a lot of factors and levels.

Perhaps the marginal_effects() function already does something like this internally?

All the best,

Oscar

messages.body_plain:
Hi Oscar,

from what I understand of your question, marginal_effects does exactly what you want. Maybe you did not realise that it does not only plot, it also returns the marginal effects.

so assign
group_means = marginal_effects(your_model)

and inspect the resulting data frame.

Also check ?marginal_effects if you want to do more complex stuff with it (but the things you mention should work directly).

Best,

Ruben

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Calculating group means from model coefficients - Is there a quick way to do it?
messages.subject_clean: [brms-users] Calculating group means from model coefficients - Is there a quick way to do it?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ruben,

Thanks for the speedy reply!

So I would just access these like this?:

group_means = marginal_effects(post1)
group_means$`A:B`

Is there anyway to get all the samples, rather than just a summary?

Many thanks for your help.

Oscar

On Thursday, 5 October 2017 12:50:04 UTC+1, Ruben Arslan wrote:
> Hi Oscar,
>
>
> from what I understand of your question, marginal_effects does exactly what you want. Maybe you did not realise that it does not only plot, it also returns the marginal effects.
>
> so assign
> group_means = marginal_effects(your_model)
>
> and inspect the resulting data frame.
>
> Also check ?marginal_effects if you want to do more complex stuff with it (but the things you mention should work directly).
>
> Best,
>
> Ruben
>
> On Thu, Oct 5, 2017 at 1:45 PM Oscar Giles <oscart...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I've finally been persuaded to switch from Python to R for fitting regression models because BRMS is so awesomel!!
> >
> >
> > However, i'm a little rusty with R, so this is a noob question.
> >
> >
> > What I would like to be able to do is quickly calculate means of every level of multiple factors quickly, in order to do hypothesis testing and plotting.
> >
> >
> > Let me clarify with an example. Say a have data set with two factors, each with two levels:
> >
> > data = data.frame(
> >     A = rep(c("A1", "A2"), each = 10),
> >     B = c("B1", "B2"),
> >     Y = rnorm(20, 0, 1)
> > )
> >
> >
> > I then fit a simple fixed effects model using brms,
> >
> > post1 = brm(Y ~ A * B, data = data)
> >
> >
> > Now I can extract the posterior samples for the fixed effects,
> >
> > feff = head(posterior_samples(post1, 'b'))
> >
> > and it would look something like this:
> >
> >   b_Intercept      b_AA2     b_BB2  b_AA2:BB2
> > 1  -1.3444522 0.99164610 1.2801640 -1.3762587
> > 2  -0.8593994 0.55953183 0.9143220 -0.7234478
> > 3  -0.6114819 0.25175212 0.2485278 -0.3393085
> > 4  -0.6324323 0.08866249 0.5348998 -0.4742578
> >
> >
> > Now say if I wanted to calculate the group mean for A1:B2, i would sum across the "b_Intercept" and "b_BB2" columns. Or I could multiply each row by c(1, 0, 1, 0).
> >
> > Another way I could do this it to call,
> >
> >  hypothesis(post1, "Intercept + BB2 = 0")
> >
> > which returns the mean estimate and intervals.
> >
> >
> > What I'd like to know is if there is a quick way of obtaining the samples. For example, is there a function that would let me say something like:
> >
> > get_identity_vector(A = A1, B = B2) which would return c(1,0,1,0). Manually specifying the vector is quite time consuming once there are a lot of factors and levels.
> >
> >
> > Perhaps the marginal_effects() function already does something like this internally?
> >
> >
> >
> > All the best,
> >
> > Oscar
> >
> >
> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
There is no p-value for LOO comparisons and no "significance" either. If desparately want to have some threshold, you could use 2*SEs as a rule of thumb. So whenver a difference is 2*SE (of the difference) away from zero it is something substantial, but please don't overstate this rule.

In your case you have a difference of ~41 with an SE of ~19 so according to our rule, the model including the random effects (fit5) clearly fits better.

With regard to the SD / Var question, I made a mistake in my code. It should be

colMeans(posterior_samples(<your model object>, pars = "^sd_")^2)

messages.subject: Ordered probit model with (multiplicative) heteroscedastic error
messages.subject_clean: Ordered probit model with (multiplicative) heteroscedastic error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

Amazing work with the package so far. I have a question about fitting an ordered probit regression model, with an additional scale parameter, using brms' nonlinear formula syntax.

You might know that I recently wrote two blog posts about estimating probit regression models to binary data (using brms' nonlinear syntax). In Psychology, these models are extremely common, and known as Signal Detection Theory models if the data is coded in a specific way. The blog posts are here (links to relevant sections):

Non-hierarchical model:
https://vuorre.netlify.com/post/2017/bayesian-estimation-of-signal-detection-theory-models-part-1/#estimate-evsdt-with-a-nonlinear-model

Hierarchical model:
https://vuorre.netlify.com/post/2017/bayesian-estimation-of-signal-detection-theory-models-part-2/#estimation-with-a-glmm-nonlinear-syntax

These models deal with binary 0/1 responses. Commonly, psychologists wish to fit these models to rating responses instead (e.g. Y = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}), which can be done with ordinal probit models. This can be (remarkably) easily done with brms. However, writing out the nonlinear brms syntax for the ordinal probit model escapes my brms skills. The nonlinear syntax implementation would be extremely valuable, because this would allow including an additional scale parameter inside the link function, leading to a common generalization of the model.

It is quite easy to modify the generated stan code from the simpler model to include the scale parameter, so I am hoping that brms could generate the code directly--I just can't figure out the syntax.

I have been unable to figure out the brms nonlinear syntax for the model, and am hoping you could help. The problem is somewhat involved, so I have posted a reproducible example of this on github: https://github.com/mvuorre/uvsdt-brms You can take a look at the repo, which contains test data, and an implementation of the desired model by modifying the brms-generated Stan code.

I think this would be an extremely useful model for psychologists (and many other fields that use signal detection models). Especially if it'd be possible to fit it with nonlinear syntax, which would allow easily fitting hierarchical versions of the model.

I am happy to submit an issue on GitHub if you'd prefer that.

Thanks so much for your hard work on the package. It's already having a big impact in applied community.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matti,

first of all thanks for writing these amazing blog posts! I really enjoyed reading them! :-)

The non-linear syntax is not activated for ordinal models, because of the way intercepts (often called thresholds) have to be dealt with in ordinal models, effectively interfering with the non-linear syntax.

I cannot access the github page right now, but maybe the "disc" parameter of ordinal models is of help. It can be prediced in the same way as, for instance, the residual SD sigma in normal models.
'disc' allows changing the discrimination parameter of the ordinal model (the names comes from item response theory), without having to use the non-linear syntax. Is this, by chance, the scale parameter you have in mind?

Best,
Paul

> Hi Paul,
>
> Amazing work with the package so far. I have a question about fitting an ordered probit regression model, with an additional scale parameter, using brms' nonlinear formula syntax.
>
> You might know that I recently wrote two blog posts about estimating probit regression models to binary data (using brms' nonlinear syntax). In Psychology, these models are extremely common, and known as Signal Detection Theory models if the data is coded in a specific way. The blog posts are here (links to relevant sections):
>
> Non-hierarchical model:
> https://vuorre.netlify.com/post/2017/bayesian-estimation-of-signal-detection-theory-models-part-1/#estimate-evsdt-with-a-nonlinear-model
>
> Hierarchical model:
> https://vuorre.netlify.com/post/2017/bayesian-estimation-of-signal-detection-theory-models-part-2/#estimation-with-a-glmm-nonlinear-syntax
>
> These models deal with binary 0/1 responses. Commonly, psychologists wish to fit these models to rating responses instead (e.g. Y = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}), which can be done with ordinal probit models. This can be (remarkably) easily done with brms. However, writing out the nonlinear brms syntax for the ordinal probit model escapes my brms skills. The nonlinear syntax implementation would be extremely valuable, because this would allow including an additional scale parameter inside the link function, leading to a common generalization of the model.
>
> It is quite easy to modify the generated stan code from the simpler model to include the scale parameter, so I am hoping that brms could generate the code directly--I just can't figure out the syntax.
>
> I have been unable to figure out the brms nonlinear syntax for the model, and am hoping you could help. The problem is somewhat involved, so I have posted a reproducible example of this on github: https://github.com/mvuorre/uvsdt-brms You can take a look at the repo, which contains test data, and an implementation of the desired model by modifying the brms-generated Stan code.
>
> I think this would be an extremely useful model for psychologists (and many other fields that use signal detection models). Especially if it'd be possible to fit it with nonlinear syntax, which would allow easily fitting hierarchical versions of the model.
>
> I am happy to submit an issue on GitHub if you'd prefer that.
>
> Thanks so much for your hard work on the package. It's already having a big impact in applied community.
>
>

Sorry, I had the github repo in 'private' mode (?), but it is public now: https://github.com/mvuorre/uvsdt-brms

I am not familiar with IRT or how the discrimination parameter works in those models. Nevertheless, I gave it a shot and, remarkably, it seems to be exactly what I wanted. I have added the code into the example on github, in case you are interested.

Looking at the produced Stan code, it now makes sense. I did not pay attention to the "disc" parameter (which is included and set to 1 if not predicted), but it is basically the inverse of the scale parameter that I am trying to include. I'll read a bit more about IRT and will write this up as a blog post some time soon. If brms/Stan does a good job of estimating the hierarchical version of this model (I have no reason to expect it won't), this will be a remarkably useful set of models for applied work in psychology and other fields that use signal detection theory. In fact, I think SPSS can't estimate the hierarchical version of this model, and other SDT specific packages certainly can't.

Thanks Paul!

messages.body_plain:
It works well! I have a follow up question, though: Is it possible to fit category-specific (that is, intercept-specific) standard deviations?

I have data with 6 response categories, so want five population level and group-level intercepts. Here’s the syntax:
model1 <- bf(rating ~ isold + (isold |s| id),
                    disc ~ 0 + isold + (0 + isold |s| id))

fit1 <- brm(model1,
                 family = cumulative(link="probit"),
                 data = d,
                 prior = Prior,
                 control = list(adapt_delta = .9), inits = 0,
                 cores = 4)

This works (takes about 5 hours for 97 groups and 46000 data points, on 4 cores with default iterations). However, as far as I know, brms doesn’t allow ‘category-specific effects’ with family = cumulative, and there is therefore only one standard deviation for the group-level intercepts:
summary(fit1)
Group-Level Effects:
~id (Number of levels: 97)
                          Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
sd(Intercept)                 0.49      0.03     0.42     0.56        365 1.02
sd(isold)                     1.01      0.08     0.87     1.17        559 1.00
sd(disc_isold)                0.58      0.04     0.51     0.67        511 1.01
cor(Intercept,isold)         -0.72      0.05    -0.81    -0.61        451 1.00
cor(Intercept,disc_isold)     0.70      0.05     0.59     0.80        477 1.01
cor(isold,disc_isold)        -0.85      0.03    -0.91    -0.79        574 1.00

Population-Level Effects:
             Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
Intercept[1]    -0.68      0.05    -0.78    -0.59        218 1.01
Intercept[2]     0.25      0.05     0.16     0.35        216 1.01
Intercept[3]     0.75      0.05     0.65     0.84        216 1.01
Intercept[4]     1.14      0.05     1.04     1.24        217 1.01
Intercept[5]     1.71      0.05     1.61     1.81        223 1.01
isold            1.44      0.10     1.24     1.63        210 1.01
disc_isold      -0.31      0.06    -0.42    -0.20        261 1.01

I think this model is reasonable (could play around with a little more to get more eff.samples), but perhaps one might want to fit a model with separate standard deviations for the five group-level intercepts. Is that possible with brms? I think this more parsimonious model is better in some sense, but it might be worth exploring the more complex one as well.

Cheers!

messages.body_plain:
The reasons, brms does not allow category specific effets for the cumulative family is not because I didn't implement it (in fact I just had to change one check so that the model started sampling). The problem is the category specific effects in the cumulative model can imply negative probabilities, which will cause Stan to (rightly) fail immediately. Since we are exploring the full posterior distribution, chances that a probability is negative at some point is almost 100%.

ML approaches might sometimes work, if the ML estimate itself as well as its transition to this estimate from the starting values all stay within positive probabilites, but this is pure luck and tends to be pretty unstable.

If you want to use category specifc effects, you should go for the sratio, cratio, or acat family, but I am aware that those models will likely not fit into the signal detection framework.

> category specific effects in the cumulative model can imply negative
> probabilities, which will cause Stan to (rightly) fail immediately. Since
> we are exploring the full posterior distribution, chances that a
> probability is negative at some point is almost 100%.
>
> ML approaches might sometimes work, if the ML estimate itself as well as
> its transition to this estimate from the starting values all stay within
> positive probabilites, but this is pure luck and tends to be pretty
> unstable.
>
> If you want to use category specifc effects, you should go for the sratio,
> cratio, or acat family, but I am aware that those models will likely not
> fit into the signal detection framework.

messages.subject: How to scale parameters
messages.subject_clean: How to scale parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am using brms to fit a Weibull growth model.

When I specify it as:

weibull.bf2 <- bf(
  height ~ Hmax - (Hmax - Hmin) * exp(-((k)*days)^delta), #Weibull model
  Hmax + k + delta ~ (1|ID),
  Hmin ~ 1,
  nl=TRUE)

Then the parameter k ends up being very small and leads to sampling problems.

To put k on a more similar scale to the rest of the parameters I changed the model so that k was being divided by 100 in the formula:

weibull.bf3 <- bf(
  height ~ Hmax - (Hmax - Hmin) * exp(-((k/100)*days)^delta), #Weibull model
  Hmax + k + delta ~ (1|ID),
  Hmin ~ 1,
  nl=TRUE)

This works well.  But is this best way to accomplish the scaling or should I be doing something else?

Thanks,

Julin

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit a zero inflated poisson model, very similar to the one in the distributional modes vignette: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/brms/vignettes/brms_distreg.html

The main difference is that I am trying to include an exposure/offset. Fitting the model without the offset goes quickly with no trouble (low Rhat).

At 2000 iterations, the model appears to fit fine, with Rhat=1 and sensible parameter estimates. When I try 4000 iterations, the model has high Rhat values and says that max_treedepth has been reached. I tried the model on the default tree depth of 10 and 12. I tried with 15 but after 45 minutes the model wouldn't fit.

Furthermore, fitting the model in the rethinking package, even with 4000 iterations, I get similar parameter estimates as the 2000 iteration model.

Anyone have any perspective what might be going on? Have a misspecified the brms model somehow? Any advice on debugging?

Here is the minimum working code and output to show this effect:

library(brms)
library(rethinking) # for data
data(Fish)
d <- Fish

rstan_options (auto_write=TRUE)
options (mc.cores=parallel::detectCores ()) # Run on multiple cores

mod.brms.2000 <- brm(bf(fish_caught ~ persons + camper + child + offset(log(hours)),
                   zi ~ child),
                data=d, family=zero_inflated_poisson(),
                prior = c(set_prior("normal(0,10)", class = 'b'),
                          set_prior("normal(0,10)", class = 'Intercept')),
                iter=2000)

summary(mod.brms.2000)

#  Family: zero_inflated_poisson
#   Links: mu = log; zi = logit
# Formula: fish_caught ~ persons + camper + child + offset(log(hours))

# Population-Level Effects:

# Samples were drawn using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Eff.Sample
# is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential
# scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

mod.brms.4000 <- brm(bf(fish_caught ~ persons + camper + child + offset(log(hours)),
                   zi ~ child),
                data=d, family=zero_inflated_poisson(),
                prior = c(set_prior("normal(0,10)", class = 'b'),
                          set_prior("normal(0,10)", class = 'Intercept')),
                iter=4000, control=list(max_treedepth=12))

summary(mod.brms.4000)

messages.body_plain:
I tried fitting the model a few different times using the random seed method described in the brms manual. The mean value of zi_child is less extreme, but still has a very large Rhat.

I'm also still getting this warning about max tree depth:

Warning messages:

1: There were 2385 transitions after warmup that exceeded the maximum treedepth. Increase max_treedepth above 12. See

http://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#maximum-treedepth-exceeded <http://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#maximum-treedepth-exceeded>

2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems

Stan also recommends examining the pairs plot. The marginal posterior distribution for b_zi_child does look very weird. The weirdness disappears when I remove the offset term, which makes me think there is something going on with that. Here is the output without the offset:

mod.brms <- brm(bf(fish_caught ~ persons + camper + child,

zi ~ child),

                iter=4000, seed = sample(1e+7, size = 1))

messages.subject: ask about normalization of predictors in three-level logistic model
messages.subject_clean: ask about normalization of predictors in three-level logistic model
messages.body_plain:
Dears,

Hello, recently I tried to build up a three-level logistic model (individual--subdistrict--district) and estimate effects of contextual predictors through brms packages. Considering others' suggestions, I did grand-centering on individual predictors and contextual predictors of subdistricts, and did group-centering on contextual predictors of districts. And to excluding the scale influences, I normalized all predictors using z-score method (with mean=0, sd=1), and then input them in brm().  However, when I checked the stan code behind, and found that it had already done group-centering (on contextual predictors of subdistricts) during the process but it seems that it didn't incorporate normalization (?). Therefore, it might cause some problem to do centering and normalization before estimation, right? If so, how can I do? Many thanks.

Regards.

Diva

> Hello, recently I tried to build up a three-level logistic model (individual--subdistrict--district) and estimate effects of contextual predictors through brms packages. Considering others' suggestions, I did grand-centering on individual predictors and contextual predictors of subdistricts, and did group-centering on contextual predictors of districts. And to excluding the scale influences, I normalized all predictors using z-score method (with mean=0, sd=1), and then input them in brm().  However, when I checked the stan code behind, and found that it had already done group-centering (on contextual predictors of subdistricts) during the process but it seems that it didn't incorporate normalization (?). Therefore, it might cause some problem to do centering and normalization before estimation, right? If so, how can I do? Many thanks.
>
> Regards.
>
> Diva

messages.body_snippet: You don't have to worry about the centering done internally. This is just to improve convergence and does **not** affect the estimates. Thus you can just center (and normalize etc.) however you like.
